extracted.intended_audience: journalists, political communicators, policymakers, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for creating and deploying public symbols, statements, and organized choices to shape mass opinion—covering phrasing, timing, messengers, media, and organizational presentation of Yes/No choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and control of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: He who captures the symbols by which public feeling is for the moment contained, controls by that much the approaches of public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To influence policy you must identify and capture the symbols that currently contain public feeling; possession of those symbols gives leverage over the 'approaches' of public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid violent abuse or overuse of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Too violent abuse of the actualities which groups of people think the symbol represents, or too great resistance in the name of that symbol to new purposes, will, so to speak, burst the symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor resonance and avoid pushing a symbol beyond what the public's experience will tolerate; overreach or rigid repurposing can destroy its unifying power (example: Holy Russia in 1917).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit modern communication machinery to create common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: It was an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication to start a return to a 'common consciousness' throughout the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available mass communication technologies (cable, telegraph, daily press, radio) to disseminate the same ideas/names for ideas simultaneously and to knit disparate publics together; without such machinery certain experiments would be impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design documents to convey precision and business-like authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The numbering of them was an artifice to secure precision, and to create at once the impression that here was a business-like document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and presentation (e.g., clear numbering, business-like phrasing) are rhetorical devices to convey seriousness and precision and to make a public statement more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft terms broad enough to unite but limited enough to avoid capture
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms had to be such that the majority among the Allies would regard them as worth while. They had to meet the national aspirations of each people, and yet to limit those aspirations so that no one nation would regard itself as a catspaw for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate language that appeals to multiple constituencies simultaneously—meeting varied aspirations while constraining extreme claims; balance inclusiveness and limitation to preserve coalition unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfy both official interests and popular conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms had to satisfy official interests so as not to provoke official disunion, and yet they had to meet popular conceptions so as to prevent the spread of demoralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When framing public policy language, ensure it is acceptable to governing elites (to keep official unity) while resonating with popular sentiment (to maintain morale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proposals plausible and actionable (terms of a possible peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: But they had also to be the terms of a possible peace, so that in case the German center and left were ripe for agitation, they would have a text with which to smite the governing class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely aspirational rhetoric; craft proposals that opponents and third parties can plausibly act on or rally around—this gives rhetorical leverage and practical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols rooted in shared experience rather than abstract omnibus phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: As you go further away from experience, you go higher into generalization or subtlety... with some phrase like the Rights of Humanity ... you see far and wide, but you see very little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbols tied to concrete, familiar experiences (e.g., 'France') rather than broad abstractions ('Europe', 'Rights of Humanity') if you need durable emotional attachment and clear public meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words with meticulous care to cover contingencies and signal audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word here was chosen with meticulous care... The word 'righted' guaranteed satisfaction to France, but did not read as a commitment to simple annexation... By insistence on '1871' the President was really defining the ultimate boundary...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select phrasing that can satisfy different expectations and strategically signal particular audiences or historical references; use ambiguity intentionally to cover multiple contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer a competing spectacle or narrative to divert attention
rubrics_metrics.description: It was an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication to start a public world-wide debate...They were intended to compete for attention by substituting for the spectacle of Russo-German parleys the much grander spectacle of a public world-wide debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an opposing narrative dominates, introduce an alternative public performance or narrative that re-frames attention and establishes a different agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce symbols through authoritative, strategically placed messengers at opportune moments
rubrics_metrics.description: The words themselves do not crystallize random feeling. The words must be spoken by people who are strategically placed, and they must be spoken at the opportune moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The messenger and timing are essential: deploy symbols via figures recognized as authoritative by the target audience and at moments when publics are receptive; otherwise language will be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility requires trusted reporters or advisers when facts are out of sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Except on a few subjects where our own knowledge is great, we cannot choose between true and false accounts. So we choose between trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When audiences lack direct knowledge, ensure information is transmitted by sources they recognize as trustworthy (editors, advisers, familiar institutions) to increase acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical communication often favors accessible authority over abstruse experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The people on whom we depend for contact with the outer world are those who seem to be running it... The experts themselves are not in the least certain... the expert... is likely as not too busy to be consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While technical experts are ideal, messages intended for mass publics often rely on visible leaders or organizational heads who are accessible and whose authority is recognized by audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present concrete Yes/No choices to mobilize mass decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of direct action is for all practical purposes the power to say Yes or No on an issue presented to the mass... A concrete choice had to be presented, the choice had to be connected, by the transfer of interest through the symbols, with individual opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame issues in simple, binary or clearly delineated choices (e.g., vote for/against) linked to the symbol(s) to translate varied private motives into a unified public decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use organized hierarchies or machines to formulate and present choices
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of heads present a choice to a large group... The professional politicians learned this long before the democratic philosophers. And so they organized the caucus, the nominating convention, and the steering committee, as the means of formulating a definite choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on organizational structures (caucuses, steering committees, editorial boards) to convert diffuse opinions into a single public option; mass publics rarely self-organize explicit policy choices without such intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of making phrases 'all things to all men'—emotion can be stirred while meaning disperses
rubrics_metrics.description: As the public appeal becomes more and more all things to all men, as the emotion is stirred while the meaning is dispersed, their very private meanings are given a universal application... soon comes to mean pretty nearly everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While broad phrasing can rally many groups, excessive generality dilutes specific meaning; balance emotional inclusivity with enough concrete content so expectations are not universally inflated and later disappointed.
